subtype: Literal, figurative and posed communication at work [Interpreting]
passage: So the email from Aparna said, "Wonderful, another Friday deadline. Love that for us." I'm Rukmini, I handle vendor orders, and I read it three times. Was she angry about my late request? Was it a joke? Her emails are usually very plain. My first draft reply was stiff. Something like, "Noted, will avoid future delays." Then I stopped, because if she was joking I'd sound like a robot, and if she was upset I'd be pretending not to notice. So I walked over and said, "Your email, was that a sigh or a dig?" She laughed and said it was a sigh at the calendar, not at me. Honestly, I felt silly, and also glad I hadn't sent the stiff one.

qa.q: What did Rukmini's first draft reply say?
qa.a: It said something like "Noted, will avoid future delays."

qa.q: What was Rukmini worried about before sending anything?
qa.a: Rukmini worried about sounding like a robot if Aparna was joking, or seem to ignore real upset if Aparna was annoyed. Aparna's emails are usually plain, which made this one hard to read.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who can't tell whether an email is sarcastic?
qa.a: Check the intent kindly with a short, friendly question before replying defensively. Rukmini's "sigh or a dig" question did exactly this.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt if Rukmini had sent the stiff reply?
qa.a: Aparna, who was sighing at the calendar, might have felt puzzled or even hurt that a shared groan was taken as blame.

grounding: Illustrates reading a possibly sarcastic or figurative work email and checking the intent instead of assuming.

subtype: Literal, figurative and posed communication at work [Interpreting]
passage:
I sit two desks from Tushar, so I saw the whole thing, or at least the outside of it. He opened an email, read it, and went quiet. His jaw tightened a little. He typed something, deleted it, typed again, deleted again. I glanced at his screen by accident, and the line was: Thanks for your "thorough" update. It could have been a dig about the length. It could also just be a manager's way of praising, with the quotation marks meaning nothing. I honestly couldn't tell, and I'm not sure he could either. After about ten minutes he stood up and walked to the manager's desk. I didn't hear it. He came back, breathed out, and said only, "She meant it. She wanted more of them." I still don't know exactly what he had been thinking.
— Omkar

qa.q: How many desks away does Omkar sit from Tushar?
qa.a: Omkar sits two desks from Tushar.

qa.q: What might Tushar have been thinking as he typed and deleted his reply?
qa.a: Most likely he was unsure whether the quotation marks around "thorough" were criticism and didn't want to answer wrongly. He might equally have been just choosing polite wording, and Omkar can't know for sure.

qa.q: What small step helped Tushar settle his doubt about the email?
qa.a: He walked to the manager's desk and asked directly, and came back knowing she meant it as praise.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt if Tushar had replied coldly?
qa.a: The manager, who meant it as praise, might have been confused by a cold reply and wondered what had gone wrong.

grounding: Illustrates an email remark that could be literal, figurative or sarcastic, where checking intent avoids needless conflict, seen by a coworker.

subtype: Literal, figurative and posed communication at work [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday. Chaitanya's email lands at 9:40: "Great, the launch moved again. Love it." Madhuri reads it three times. She was the one who asked the client for the extra week. Her jaw tightens. She types a sharp reply about "doing my job," then saves it as a draft and closes the laptop.

Wednesday. On the team call she unmutes. "Chaitanya, quick one. Was Monday's email about my request? I couldn't tell if it was sarcastic." He blinks, then laughs. "Half sarcastic, at the client, who keeps changing their mind. The extra week actually saves me. Sorry, I should have written that."

The following Monday. A new email: "Sure, that'll be easy." Madhuri doesn't brood. She pings him: "Easy-easy or ironic-easy?" He replies, "Ironic, but doable 🙂." She deletes the old draft.

qa.q: At what time did Chaitanya's email arrive on Monday?
qa.a: Chaitanya's email lands at 9:40.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she first read the email, and what other reading was possible?
qa.a: She felt stung and defensive, reading it as sarcasm aimed at her request, shown by her tightening jaw and sharp draft; it could equally have been a joke about the client, which it turned out to be.

qa.q: Which choice prevented a conflict, and why?
qa.a: Saving the sharp reply as a draft and asking Chaitanya directly on Wednesday prevented a fight, because it checked his intent instead of assuming it.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt if Madhuri had sent the sharp reply?
qa.a: He would probably have been surprised and hurt, since he meant the sarcasm at the client and the extra week actually helped him.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional unsure whether a work email is literal or sarcastic and checking intent to avoid a needless conflict.

subtype: Literal, figurative and posed communication at work [Interpreting]
passage:
Sit, Shalini, this one's about that email you're glaring at.

When I was about your age, my manager, a very dry man named Kurian, sent back my first proposal with one line: "Feel free to burn the whole draft."

I was insulted. I spent that evening writing a resignation letter in my head. I thought, he's calling my work rubbish in the rudest way possible.

Next morning my senior, a patient woman in accounts, said, "Ojas, you don't know what he meant. Go and ask." So I did, voice shaking. "Sir, did you mean the draft was bad?"

Kurian looked puzzled. "The client changed the brief last night. I meant literally start again. The draft was fine for the old brief."

I nearly quit over a sentence that was just an instruction. So before you reply to that email, ask what they meant.

qa.q: What did Kurian's one-line reply say?
qa.a: It said, "Feel free to burn the whole draft."

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he first read Kurian's line, and what does it show?
qa.a: Ojas felt insulted and hurt, enough to imagine a resignation letter, which shows Ojas read a figurative insult into what was actually a literal instruction.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ojas's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: The turning point was going to ask Kurian directly the next morning; it mattered because it revealed the brief had changed and stopped Ojas from quitting over a misreading.

qa.q: How did Kurian seem to see the situation when Ojas asked him?
qa.a: Kurian looked puzzled, because to him the line was just a practical instruction about a changed brief, not a judgement of the work.

grounding: It illustrates a young professional reading a remark as a figurative insult and learning that checking intent avoids a needless conflict.

subtype: Literal, figurative and posed communication at work [Interpreting]
passage:
The train was slowing for the tunnel when Madhav's phone buzzed. His manager, Francis: "Nice work on the deck. Really bold choices."

The client meeting was at eleven, forty minutes away, and the signal bar was already flickering.

Bold. Was that praise? Or the polite way Francis said "too much"? Madhav remembered him once calling a messy chart "adventurous" with a straight face. His thumb hovered over the file. He could redo the colour scheme on the train, strip the big photos, play it safe.

Instead, before the bars vanished, he typed: "Quick check: bold good, or bold tone-it-down? Happy to adjust before 11."

The train went dark. He sat with the question for six long minutes.

At the next station the reply arrived: "Good bold. Keep it. The client asked for something that stands out." Madhav breathed out and closed the laptop.

qa.q: What time was the client meeting?
qa.a: The client meeting was at eleven.

qa.q: How can you tell Madhav was anxious about Francis's message?
qa.a: His thumb hovered over the file and he considered redoing the deck, and the six minutes felt long; he was anxious that "bold" might be polite criticism, though it could equally be real praise.

qa.q: What did Madhav do that a wise person would copy?
qa.a: Instead of redesigning based on a guess, he sent a short question to check whether "bold" was praise or a hint, and waited for the answer.

qa.q: What would change if Francis's answer had been "tone it down"?
qa.a: Madhav would still have had time to adjust before eleven, so asking would have helped either way.

grounding: It shows a young professional unsure whether a remark is literal praise or sarcasm and checking intent under time pressure instead of assuming.

subtype: Literal, figurative and posed communication at work [Interpreting]
passage: The email from Pallavi arrived at 9:02: "Loved the deck. Very bold choices on slide 4. 🔥" Divyansh read it three times at his desk in the Gurugram office. Bold as in brave, or bold as in too much? His teammate Rhea leaned over. "Fire means she's roasting you," she said. "Or it means it's hot. Who knows." Divyansh started typing a defensive reply about why the orange background matched the client's colours, then stopped. Last week Pallavi had written "Can we take a stab at a shorter version?" and he had spent a whole night cutting slides when she had meant two minutes of trimming. He walked over to her cabin instead. "Quick check on slide 4. When you said bold, did you mean it works, or it's too loud?" Pallavi laughed. "It works! I just want the font a size smaller so the client can read it from the back." Divyansh went back and changed one setting.

qa.q: What did Pallavi want changed on slide 4?
qa.a: Pallavi wanted the font a size smaller so the client could read it from the back.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh stop typing the defensive reply, and what was he feeling?
qa.a: Divyansh felt anxious and defensive about "bold choices", but remembered losing a night over "take a stab", so he doubted his first reading and chose to check.

qa.q: What could Divyansh keep doing when a work message feels unclear?
qa.a: Ask a short, specific question about what the writer meant, as he did at Pallavi's cabin, before reacting to a guess.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt if she had received the defensive reply?
qa.a: Pallavi might have been confused and a little hurt, since she meant the fire emoji as praise, and a simple font request could have turned into a needless argument.

grounding: Shows a young professional unsure whether a remark is literal, figurative or sarcastic, and checking intent instead of assuming.
